You use the infinitive with “zu” (Ich versuche, … zu …), purpose with “um … zu” and “ohne … zu”, and expressions like “Es ist wichtig, … zu …”.
to take the dog for a walk
Kuba is trying to persuade his parents.
He's saving money to buy a dog.
It's important to take the dog for a walk every day.
Use “zu + infinitive” after certain verbs (versuchen, vergessen, vorhaben, anfangen, aufhören, beschließen).
Use “zu + infinitive” after expressions (Es ist wichtig / schwer / schön, … zu …; Ich habe Lust / Zeit, … zu …).
Put “zu” in the right place with separable verbs: anzurufen, mitzukommen, aufzustehen.
Express purpose with “um … zu” and absence with “ohne … zu”.
Know that “zu” is NOT used after modal verbs.
It's January. Kuba, now eight, has a plan to get a dog. He comes to Mara to ask for her help.
Mara, can you help me? I'm planning to persuade my parents. I want a dog.
A dog? That's a big responsibility, Kuba. Have you already tried talking to them about it?
A hundred times! Mum says the flat is too small. Dad says I'll definitely forget to feed it.
No! I've been taking Fritz for a walk every day for a year, without missing a single day. In the snow too. And on my birthday.
That's true. That's a good argument. What's your plan?
I'm saving my pocket money to pay for the food myself. I've already got forty-three euros. And I've started reading books about dogs.
Wow. That's impressive. And why do you need me?
Because Mum believes everything you say. You're a nurse. Can you tell her that having a dog is healthy?
Ha! You're clever. It's actually true: walking every day is good for your health. But I'll only do it on one condition.
You promise not to buy a dog, but to adopt one from the shelter. Lots of dogs there are waiting to find a family.
I promise! And Ola? Do I have to promise her too that we'll share the dog?
You have to decide that yourself. But I think it would be wise.
“Gassi gehen” = to take the dog for a walk
“anzurufen” = “AN-tsoo-roo-fen”: “zu” sits between the prefix and the verb and is unstressed.
“Gassi gehen” = “GAH-see GAY-en”: a colloquial expression, used only for dogs.
After many verbs, the second verb comes in the infinitive with “zu” in front of it, at the END of the sentence. There's usually a comma before it:
Ich habe vergessen, ihn zu füttern.
Ich habe vor, nach Wien zu fahren.
I'm planning to go to Vienna.
Er fängt an, Bücher zu lesen.
Wir haben beschlossen, einen Hund zu adoptieren.
We've decided to adopt a dog.
Er verspricht, jeden Tag Gassi zu gehen.
He promises to take the dog out every day.

After MODAL verbs (können, müssen, wollen, dürfen, sollen, möchten) you DON'T use “zu”: “Ich will einen Hund haben”, not “zu haben”. The same goes after werden, lassen, gehen, hören, sehen. Careful: English says “I want TO have”, German doesn't!
Es ist wichtig, viel Wasser zu trinken.
It's important to drink lots of water.
Es ist schwer, Deutsch zu lernen.
Es macht Spaß, mit Fritz zu spielen.
It's fun to play with Fritz.
Ich habe Lust, ins Kino zu gehen.
I feel like going to the cinema.
Ich habe keine Zeit, zu kochen.
I don't have time to cook.
With separable verbs, “zu” goes BETWEEN the prefix and the verb, all in one word:
Do you feel like coming too?
It's hard to get up at four.
“um … zu” expresses purpose (in order to, to). It answers the question “Wozu?” or “Warum?”:
Kuba is saving money to pay for the food.
I'm learning German to work in Berlin.
Lena gets up at four to bake bread.
Kuba takes the dog out every day, without missing a single day.
“um … zu” is only used when the subject is the same. If it's different, you use “damit”: “Ich spare, damit mein Sohn einen Hund bekommt.”
He's saving money to buy a dog.
Ich will einen Hund zu haben.
Ich will zu einen Hund haben.
Ich lerne Deutsch, ___ in Berlin zu arbeiten.
I try to study every day.
dass die Wohnung zu klein ist
dass Kuba vergisst, den Hund zu füttern
Wie viel Geld hat Kuba gespart?
einen Hund aus dem Tierheim zu adoptieren

It took three weeks to persuade his parents. Kuba took Fritz for a walk every day to show he was reliable. He read three books about dogs and at dinner talked so much about dog breeds, dog food and vaccinations that Ola started covering her ears. He kept on saving. In the end he had sixty-seven euros.

Mara spoke to Kasia, as she had promised. She told her about studies showing that children with dogs get ill less often and that walking every day is good for the heart. Kasia listened and said: “Mara, I know Kuba sent you.” Mara blushed. Kasia laughed. “But you're right. And he's right too. He walked Fritz for a whole year without complaining even once. Maybe it's time.”

Piotr was harder to persuade. As a child in Poland he had had a dog, a big black shepherd dog called Burek, and when Burek died he hadn't spoken for a whole week. He didn't want his children to go through the same thing. But one Sunday evening he saw Kuba sitting on the stairs reading to Fritz from a book about dogs. Out loud, slowly, very seriously. Fritz was listening, with his head on Kuba's knee. Piotr stood in the doorway for a long time. Then he just said: “Saturday. Shelter. But you have to promise to look after him. Both of you.”

The Berlin animal shelter is on the edge of the city, in Falkenberg, and it's the biggest shelter in Europe. On Saturday morning they all went together on the S-Bahn: the whole Nowak family, Mara, who came along to help, and of course Fritz, whom Kuba wanted to take with him “to see who he likes”.

A young carer with green hair led them between the dog houses. There were so many dogs: small, big, young, old, noisy, quiet. Ola immediately fell in love with a little white puppy that looked like a cloud. Kuba stopped in front of every pen and asked about the name, the age, the story. The carer answered patiently. She seemed glad that someone was asking.

Right at the end of the corridor, in the last pen, lay a dog that didn't get up when they came. He was medium-sized and brown, with grey hair around his muzzle, one ear standing up and one hanging down. He looked at them without barking, without wagging his tail. He looked as if he had stopped hoping.
This is Bruno. He's nine. His owner was an elderly lady. She died in the autumn, and her family didn't want him. He's been here for four months. People want young dogs. Nobody asks about Bruno.

At that moment something strange happened. Fritz, who had walked quietly beside Kuba all morning, went up to the bars and pressed his nose against them. Bruno raised his head. Then he got up, slowly, went to the bars and pressed his nose against them from the other side. The two old dogs stayed like that for a whole minute, nose to nose, without making a sound.
But the little white puppy! It's so cute!
The little white puppy will find a family straight away, Ola. Everyone wants it. But Bruno… Nobody wants Bruno. It's not fair.

Ola looked at Bruno. Bruno looked at Ola. Then, very slowly, he wagged his tail. Once. Twice. Ola sighed, the way only an eight-year-old girl can sigh when she's making an important decision. “All right,” she said. “But I get to walk him every other day. And I choose the collar. A red one.”

Piotr said nothing. He knelt down in front of the bars and slowly held out his hand. Bruno sniffed it for a long time and then licked Piotr's fingers once. Mara saw Piotr get up quickly and pretend he had something in his eye.

At the shelter office they had to fill in lots of forms. The carer asked whether they had a garden, how many hours a day the dog would be alone and whether they were prepared to go to the vet regularly. Kuba answered every question before his parents could even open their mouths. When the carer asked him why he wanted an old dog of all things, he thought for a moment and said: “Because I've learned how to look after an old dog. Fritz taught me.” The carer laughed and signed. On the way home Bruno and Fritz lay side by side on the floor of the S-Bahn, and people smiled when they saw the two grey muzzles.

A week later Bruno moved into Kastanienallee. He got a red collar, a basket in the children's room, right between the two beds, and a bowl on which Kuba had written “BRUNO” in marker, with a little heart. Kuba paid for the first food with his sixty-seven euros. He insisted.

On the first evening Ludwig came round with Fritz to greet the new neighbour. The two old dogs lay down side by side on the rug in the Nowaks' hall, as if they had known each other for years. Ludwig looked at them and said to Kuba: “You know, lad, you did something important today. It's easy to love a young dog. It's harder to love an old dog. But the old ones know how to appreciate it more.” Kuba nodded seriously. He didn't understand every word. But he understood everything.
That night, for the first time in four months, Bruno slept deeply and peacefully, between two children's beds.
